query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single thermo-mechanical intervention of cryogenic rolling followed by an optimized annealing step to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine the dual-phase lamellar colonies, reduce the spacing and misorientation at internal boundaries, and thereby mitigate dislocation pile-ups that cause local stress concentrations. This processing is expected to overcome the room-temperature tensile ductility limitations and brittleness while retaining or enhancing the alloy's strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies, where coarse internal boundaries lead to dislocation pile-ups and consequential local stress concentrations, microcracking, and premature failure.
generation.intervention: Cryogenic rolling (cryo-deformation) followed by a tailored annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing after processing; the intervention is applied at cryogenic temperatures during deformation and followed by controlled annealing to achieve desired microstructural recovery and refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined and hierarchical nano-lamellar microstructure with ultrafine grains within FCC lamellae and a stabilized B2 phase, resulting in increased boundary area and reduced stress concentration at grain interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling increases strain heterogeneity and induces finer scale deformation, which, when followed by annealing, promotes nucleation of ultrafine grains and partial recrystallization. This microstructural refinement distributes dislocations more uniformly, minimizes dislocation pile-up at interfaces, and thereby reduces local stress concentrations and crack nucleation during subsequent straining.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced tensile ductility (increased elongation to failure beyond the starting material’s limited ductility) while maintaining or potentially increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or conventionally cold-rolled and annealed eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at relatively coarse internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are primarily expected for eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloys processed under similar thermo-mechanical conditions. The effectiveness of this intervention may be less pronounced if the processing parameters are not optimized or if the alloy composition deviates substantially.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports benefits from cryogenic rolling and annealing in similar systems, the precise processing window and microstructural evolution in the specific hierarchical dual-phase system could vary, making the exact balance between strength and ductility somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a batch of the eutectic high-entropy alloy via cryogenic rolling followed by a controlled annealing treatment. Prepare a control sample processed via traditional room-temperature rolling and annealing. Characterize the resulting microstructure using electron microscopy and conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing from microstructural analysis
Distribution and density of dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed sample does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (elongation to failure) and either shows no improvement or a decrease in strength compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis reveals persistent and severe dislocation pile-ups leading to similar patterns of local stress concentrations and cracking, then the hypothesis is falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing

Abstract: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
